ON DISSENT AND ITS MINISTRY.
At a meeting held at Warrington last week, to eommemorate the union of two Dissenting churches,

ByLANDs, id. 12., who on thing, was received illtlansiastgAleeiing again and again rene wed ,- said he.. understood that the object of that gathering was two fold, filst tl commemorate the Union of Dallam-lane and Filar's-green churches, and. second, to give to the public at large some information con- cerning the policy and principle of the body of the Free Gospel cc Independent Methodist Churches.

Whether he looked upon it in regard to its general or looal aspect, it had equally his warm sympathies. (Hear, hear.) In regard to its local objects his earlier associations, and in fact some of his most cherished as- inciations, carried him tack to days when he frequently attended meetings in Friars' - green Chapel. (Cheers.) He could recollect in those days, many good men who took part in the work of the churches, ani especially one good man who was connected with Friars'-green chapel during his earlier days—he alluded to Peter Philips. (Cheers.) For Mr. Philips he had a great personal esteem, for he considered him a man of thorough christian spilt, who devoted Ms life to the fulfilment of christian duty, and who was doing his Utmost to make all the efforts in his power, in order to spread religion amongst the people of Warrington. Cheers.) He recollected alto that it was ww thirty _ .

_ years ago on the omission of the public fast which was then solemnly proclaimed, since he ventured to deliver a sermon or address in the evening of that day from the pulpit of Friars'-green Chapel. (Cheers.) To those days he looked back with satisfaction, because then he was connected with various public movement& which emaaated from that place of worship. Amongst those movements there was ths temperance movement. Which in those days was not so popular, neither did it attract so much attention as it did at present. Thirty years ago christian men at Friars'-green chapel were banded together against what they felt tohe a great evil, and an influence which prevented the spread of ehristianity. They anticipated what at the present day was a growing opinion amongst religious men of all denominations, that it mattered comparatively little what christian agency the various ohurchet of the Country brought to bear on the population, so long as the great evil of drink had so much control over the population of this country. (Cheers.) He therefore believed that the members of Friars'-green chapel all along had upheld the great principles of the temper- Inge reformation, and had fulfilled in a marked man- lier what they believed to be their duty aa christian pien in advocating the claims of temperance. (Hear, bean) Not only in regard to that great movement, but in reference to other movements he had observed 1.21013g5t the people connected with the Independent Methddists, a broad catholic spirit, belonging to men ttho sought to make themselves useful without re- ference to creeds or any sectional part of Christ's Church. (Cheers.) It was therefore satisfactory to him to take the chair on that occasion and show that he sympathised with everything that had occurred in Warrington, to increase the strength and usefulness of the body which he had reason to respest so highly. (Hear, hear.) -There was a second object of that gathering, namely that an opportunity might be af- forded, to call public attention in some measure to the principles and policy of the Independent Metho- dists. On that platform there were men who could speak with very much greater authority and know- ledge on that subject than he could, but at all events, perhaps as Chairman of that meeting, he might be allowed to say that before coming to that meeting he had read the " Testimony and principles of Union of the United Free Gospel Churches." From this work he found that in the main the body of Independent Methodists agreed With the generally received theological opinions en- tertained by other Christian Churches. But while they agreed with the doctrines and principles of the Chris. tian Churches generally, they differed from them in their policy in a special manner—a policy which was not common, and which, in fact, was very rare amongst religious communities. That difference in policy was, that they did not recognise what was called a hired ministry. (Hear, hear.) In fact, they I sought to follow what they believed was the constituni B on of the Primitive Church when, in their judgmeat,' e there was no distinction between ,the clergy and th laity, and when the ministers or bishops, or priest- hood of that church were not As paid officers. (Hear. hear.) He was bound to say that he believed a careful reading of the Scriptures, and a careful aequaintanoe With eeelesiastical as well as profane history, demon. strated that such was the constitution of the Primitive Apostolic Church. (Cheers.) He would quote a few words from a great histolian—Gibbon—who said. in his "Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire," allud- ing to the second century, "The progress of ecclesias- tical authority gave birth to the memorable distinction of the laity and clergy, which had been .unknown to the Greeks and Romans." That was the case. Amongst the Greeks and Romans the priests who offered semi- OCA were in no sense what were understood n3w-a- days as clergymen. The idea of distinction between the deny and the laity was entirely unknown in those days. It arose after the commencement of the Chris. tian era. and, accordir.g to Gibbon, it arose from the putting forward of ecclesiastical pretensions. In the year A.D. 200, we meet amongst the Christian writers with the first notice of the distinction between the Clergy and laity, which was referred to by Tertullian as being "a device of the priesthood." Until that time bishor a and deacons and ordinary members at the early Church were considered as laymen, and were not in any sense of the term priests as under• derstood now-a-days. There was no distinction between the clergy and the laity at that time, and he was prepared to admit that the policy which was laid. down in "The Testimony of the Principles of Union of the Free Gospel Churches " was, in his judgment, consistent with the early practice of the first Christian Cherishes, and with the testimony which ecclesiastical history afforded. (Cheers.) He was bound to say that at the same time, in his judgment, it was a matter which was .open to question, because we existed in a different state of society, and It might be considered whether it was absolutely neces- sary to follow the exact mode and constitution of the Primitive Church in its religious agency. At all events, they might admit that, considering the great intellectual activity, and the increasing amount of popular education, and the fact that people were very much enlightened, eompared With former generations, and also, considering the demands on our time in relation to our Worldly avocations, it was open to very serious con. pideration whether it was not to the aivantage of religions bodies that there should be a certain number Of men set apart for the work of the ministry, to be naintained by salaries or stipends. to devote their en- tire leisure to the dissemination of Christian truth. At ill events, they would admit that amongst the various religious bodies in which there was a hired ministry, they had met with clergymen and ministers who had given brilliant examples of great zeal in the cause of religion, and this country owed a great debt of grati- tude to the labours and influence of those men who were connected with a hired ministry. (Hear, hear.) He was bound to say that whilst his friends stood on what they believed to be the principles of the constitu- tion of the Christian Church, they would cheerfully admit that we all owed a debt of gratiteide to such meet, and that they would be sorry in any way to in- jure their labours or their influence as religious teachers because they were hired ministers. (Hear, bear.) That was one point upon whet they differed from the other churches, but there was an- other more material point, which, in his judgment, was much more important. They not only objected to • hired ministry but they objected In a special manner to any caste or claes, making the Service of God and His work depend upon on any Ofddal distinction. (Hear, hear) They bald lie man had gifts he ought to exercise those gifts, although he ought not be able to show that he was a successor of the apostles by virtue of the laying on of hands. (Cheers.) They said all this assumption of ecclesias- tical distinction if carried too far must tend, as it did tend, to limit the energies and restrain the activity of Christian man, He objected as much as anyone did, te any system, the effect of which would seem to cramp the epergies of active Christians. (Hear, hear.) R. was quite willing to admit what he had already adnittted that under the present circum- stances we regnired the services of ministers and teachers who alte"eld have a certain amount of training and leisure for eeeir work. So far he was quite prepared to support exhili:el systems. but he thought it was very important for that coil„vregation as I body to hold to this truth, and make a protest against any tflicial Christianity, each as doing the work of Clod by proxy in return for a certain amount of pay. In that principle he agreed with them. In past times, Within the memory of living men, we had seen bishops et the church rollin g in wealth, accumulating large same a money, and when they died, had let to theit children enorasous fortunes. That was a sort of abuse of wealth attached to the teaching of religion, and which appeared to be a system of Christian teachen seeking for wealth out of their religion. The Indepen- dent Methodist Churches protested against such a system, and they taught that rather than men should be exposed to the injury of very great wealth attached i to the teaching of religion, t was better that they ehould have no salaries at all, In protesting against such abuses be agreed with them, for it seemed to him that large sums of snony attached to the teaching of religion might be much snore useful if dissemin-,ted Over a wider area. div.p: COLONEL BIACKBURNE, 11.P.9 ON EDUCATION.

On Monday evening a meeting, to inaugurate a course of lectures, under the Cambridge University ex- tension scheme, was held at Leigh, the Bishop of Man- chester presiding. Colonel Blackburne, M.P., in moving a resolution approving of the introduction of the Cambridge University extension scheme into Leigh said that young men should remember that although they had done well in their various colleges and schools, if they did not continue to improve their minds they would fall back instead of going forward; but he hoped they would work, and take advantage of the opportunities now offered and rise on the ladder of life to distinction among their fellow-countrymen. (Cheers.) He would not say a word on politics, but he 'caked them to look at what this country had done for education. In 1840 a sum of £40,000 was voted for the purposes of education, white let year's education vote for England was £1,707,055, which wis an in- crease of £151,000 odd in one year. div.p: NORTELWICH AND THE TUI KS.

A meeting of the inhabitants of Northwich was held on Monday evening, in the Market Hall, to discuss the atrocities recently committed in Bulgaria, and to pass such resolutions as the meeting thought fit. The meeting was called by Mr. Neumann, LP., chairman of the Local Board, in response to a requisition from the inhabitants.

Mr. NRIIMANN was elected chairman on the motion of Mr. Harvey, seconded by Mr. Green. The CHAIRZSAN called upbn Mr. Dixon to read the requisition ; he (Mr. Dixon).said that it was sufficiently signed to induce the Cnairman to call the meeting. (Hear, hear.) Mr. 1. T. BMlNlvini read letters of apology for none attendance, and stated that in addition to the gentle- men, whoss letters he would read, invitations had been sent to all the members of Parliament for Mid and West-Cheshire, but with one exception they hadhis re. plied.

LIEUT.-COL. MARSHALL, wrote, stating that a pre- vious engagement prevented his attendance, and re- marked, that any resolution which may be passed in reprobation of the atrocities perpetrated by the Turks in Bulgaria, will have my warmest sympathy. (Cheers.)

The Rev. A.. BURGESS wrote, regretting his inability to show public iudignation at such inhumanity. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. J. JOuwe in his letter, said that he was vei y glad to hear that a public meeting was to be held at Northwich, to express sympathy with the christian provinces of Turkey in fighting for freedom. He • did not know how they could be reconciled, when the action of our Govern- ment had been taken by all the world as sympathy for Turkey. (Hear, hear.) England would belief all that is beet and noblest in her history if she did not speak out her mind clearly and earnestly for the weak against the strong, and the oppressed against the oppressor. (Applause.) As men and Englialauten they had a right to express their loathing of such acts as those perpetrated in Bulgaria by the Turks. (Hear, hear.) He hoped the Slavonia Provinces in Turkey would receive complete independence. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. T. Prance Hayhurst wrote saying that his feeling was that the outspoken voice of the country had already done its work, and that for the present at lewd there was no object to be gained by further ex- ' pression of opinion for their town or any other. They might leave all things now in the •hands of the Go- vernment. (Hear, hear, and oh, oh.) The time may come when there may be a fresh call for the nation to lilt up its voice, but he thought not at present. The Hon. W. Egerton wrote.—

I have observed that meetings .for a similar object have been held in different parts of the kingdom, which, though professing to be independent of politioal parties. have yet passed resolutions tending either to fetter the action of her Majesty's Government, or to make theta in seine way responsible for the action of the Turkish Government. Such a line of conduct does not pprove itself to me. I beg, therefore, to decline to attend ameeting, or to express a decided opinion on the subjk ct while we are not in possession of any Mil, cial documents to enable us to judge how far tne Turkish Government is to blame in the 'matter, , and coy rash comments on their conduct will only mike the desired restoration of peace more difficult of at- tainannit, and may possibly embarrass the action of the earl of Darby in the oonduct"of the delicate negotia- tions winch he is now carrying on in concert with the other great powers for that object.;- All must deplore deeply the melancholy occurrences in Bulgaria, and be moved with just iudignation against the perpetrators of those crimes, but we ought not unreservedly to con- demn the Turkish Government without a full know- ledge of the circumstances. 'The latest amounts show that it is fully prepaied to punish the chief actors in those atrocities, and to give redress to the sufferers. From the recent speech of Lord Derby rhave perfect confidence that he is fully impressed with the grave character and complicated nature of the Eastern Ques- tion, and believe that the interests of peace and the rights of the Chrisdan populatian Under the rule of Turkey, which have strong claims on our sympathy, will best be consulted by abstaining from any attempt to interfere with the action of the ministry at the pre- sent crisis.

Bradwall Hall, Sandbach. Dear Sir,—l am gni:bang so much from an attack of rheumatic gout that all I oan do is to walk on two stioke from one room to another. Under these circura- stances it will be impos.iole for use to come to North- wich on Monday, 18th Sept., to attend your meeting. I trust that those present at the meeting will not only join in an expression of horror at the atrocities which seems to be admitted to have happened in Bulgaria but will also urge on the Government the necessity of a change in policy. To ruji mind there is a double aspect to this question • the view of humanity and the view of public -policy. BULGARIAN ATROCITIES.

At the public) meeting held in Warrington, to denounce the Bulgarian Atrocities, last week, and which was addressed by Mr. P. Rylands, whose speech appeared in our last issue, the following speeches were also delivered :

Mr. Cimino& CEOFFIELD, the chosen Liberal candi- date for the borough, who was received with cord% and prolonged cheering, said, Ladies and Gentleme The resolution I propose to submit for your approval is one that I am quite sure will meet with the cordial approval of all who are present here to-night, and so far as regards the first part of it, the expres- sion of regret at the atrocities that have been committed in Bulgaria by the Turkish troops. I am quite confident that will meet with the approval of not only those who are present, but of a large majority of the inhabitants of this town. (Applause.) The subject for the consideration of this meeting is one which I think might have justi- fied the Mayor in taking some public action. (Hear, hear.) I had no wish to take any advantage politi- cally, fakeer individually or collectively to thb party to which I belong, for any special sympathy with those who are suffering from oppression, but I think the present resembles very much the movement of the Anti-Slavery Association, 40 years ago, when the whole population of England as one man, might ex- press their Opinion strongly in condemnation of the Wickedness and atrocities that have been perpetratekbY people whom we have to call our fellow-oreaturee, in other countries. (Cheers.) The present question scarcely amounts to a political one in England, but un- fortunately the Government do seem to have allied themselves with the Turkish Government who have sanotioned these atrocities and have rewarded the men who have coermitted them. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause,) I daresay a Government is in a difficulty when it has taken the first step—which our Governs meat did by sending our navy to Beek& Bay—and for months they kept the English public, in ignorance of their object in sending it there. (Hear, hear.) The Turkish Gov-rnment apparently have supposed that the Englieu- Government were supporting them, and they have allowed their own soldiers ro commit these atrocities, the details of which I would net venture to repeat. (kLear, hear.) Our Prime Minister when in. terrogatsa in the House of Commons with respect to these atrocities—with that skilful and adroit language and manner which we know so well—snubbed the man who asked the question and said, they were imaginary atrocities. (Hear, hear.) If it had not been for the intelligence and perseverance of the correspondent of the Daily Newa,—(oneers)— these wicked prdceedings would probably have never been known to the world, Even within the last few days—l think on Saturday last—our Foreign Society, Lord Derby, described the newspaper accounts as skillful and artistic narratives. (Applause.) It is almost impossible to imagine that in tem dajeof enlightenment, we can have a Minister in this country who can describe the terrible things we have all read of in fingsage such as that, language meant apparently to discourage express sitars of opinion on the part of the English, people. We have, however, witnessed the great wave of popular feeling manifesting itself in an uumistakable manner throughout the length and breadth of the land. , (Cheers.) To the deputation who waited on Lord , Derby the ether day ha described, as I have said, the reports of the atrocities as "skillful and artistic narra- tives." He had scarcely a word of sympathy for the poor creatures who had been so sacrificed and roasted to death. (Hear, hear.) It has nearly always been the case in this country—and he, the speaker, was sorry to 'say it—the Ooeservative party have sided with the oppressors in other countries, (Hear, hear.) it is the pride of the Liberal party that they have always sympathised with the oppressed wherever they have I been found. There is in this Eastern question no longer the same feeling which existed 24 years ago, when we unfortunately went into the Crimean war, and sacrificed forty thousand lives and a hundred i millions of money, n defence of this wretched and miserable Government of Turkey, who have now per- mitted their soldiers to commit these horrid deeds in kiulgaria. (Cheers.) The present Gsvernmeur„ in con- sequence of that Crimean war in 18th4 aria 113b6, have supported the Turkish Government against these Christian people in beryls, and committed these mill. deeds, which would shock the least cultivated people in the world. That we, as a nation, are bound up in support of a miserable government like this, which is a disgrace to the civilisation of Europe, and the age in which we live, is a public humiliation. (Cheers.) Shall Warrington, then, which has never lagged be- hind in any generous national movement; witunuld its voice in eweiriug that great wave or indignation and remonstrance which is now passing over the country, sod which must nifallab y reach that miserable bank- rupt country or Turkey f Let Warrington lift up its voice in memorialising the Queers to issue new instruc- tions to her Ambassador at Constantinople—who is in reoeipt of 03,000 a year, and yet seems to have been less informed than the correspondents of the London newspapers—(Cheere.)—Sir Fly. Elliot has lama de. scribed by the Prime Minister as an active, intelligent, and impartial observer of events—and he, although in receipt of this large income paid by the English people, could not inform them of the atrocities that were being committed. On the contrary, he rather disputed the accuracy of the accounts sent by the intelligent cor- respondent of the _Daily New, and our inthigtere in both Houses of Parliament seem to have disbelieved and disputed the truth of these statements. (Hear, hear.) It remains for us, along with all the other towns in the kingdom, to prevent the Government in the future from aiding Turkey in her nefarious enterprise. Above all things, we must strongly express our deter- mination not to permit our Government to go to warm supporting a government that has been guilty of bush atrocities. its • I beg to move "That this meet- jug records sense of horror and disgust at the ter. rible outrages committed by the Turks with the appa- teat approval of the Ottoman Government upon the unarmed population of Bulgaria, and is of opinion that the Britian Government has failed to exhibit sufficient promptitude in discovering these outrges, arid energy in regard to the adoption of toe measures which they render necessary," (Renewed cheering.)

ENGLAND AND TURKEY.

THE grotesquely Conservative spirit which prevails amongst certain sections of politi- cians in the country, is curiously illustrated by the disposition to maintain, at all hazards, what they call the Atatus quo in the Turkish mpire. The manner in which Lord Bea- consfield, and those who sympathise with him and his party, fall down before the Turk and worship that image of clay and blood which gibbers on the Bosphorus is something terrible to reasonable men. Eng- land is now paying the shocking penalty of past diplomacy, and reaping where It has so unhappily sown. We are now in the position in which our past acts have placed us. Rightly or wrongly .—it is most idle to speculate which—we up- held Turkey in Europe twenty years ago, at a great cost of life and treasure. It must be remarked that, but for us, the Ottoman had no hope At that time it was easy for us, humanly speaking, to take away his breath. so that he should die and return to his dust. Nor was it necessary to lift a finger in the matter to accomplish this. Passivity would have answered every pur- pose, had our wish been the destruction of the Turkish Empire i and the great country of the Czar—then, be it remembeL ad, much richer than it is at present—would have done the work effectively alone. England did not think fit to take that passive course, snd hence to-day she is hampered and fet- tered in her relation to this matter, by the history of the past. It is one of the condi- tions of social life, individually and nation- ally, that we cannot ignore the responsibili- ties of past conduct, any more than we can recall that past itself. At some future time, it may be useful to debate the wisdom of the Crimean war, but this is not the question of the hour, and the one which imperatively demands an immediate solution. Given such and such a condition of things, seen in the light of such and such responsibilities: what is the right course of action to take ? It is hardly denied, even by the Government, that the Eastern Question involves us in the responsibility (in Mr. Lowe's words) of knowledge of evils and power to remedy them. But our amenability to the bar of conscience and public feeling is still greater. 'We have helped to make this monstrosity— the Turkish Empire—or et least, to make it what it is. Our case is somewhat like that of Frankenstein, who, after years of toil and horrid research in charnel houses, succeeded in creating a man, organically like himself, yet not the offspring of humanity. The creature could not be killed, yet how to en- dure the loathsome "companionship ?" The story may serve for the purpose of illus- tration. From the charnelhouses, graves, and battlefields of the Crimea we have ex- tracted the essences whic enabled us to breathe new life into the Turkish monster- man. We dare not slay the creature of our hand, but all the more are we bound, by every natural and moral obligation, to re- strain and curb it. Indications are not want- ing that the inertia of the Government is producing the effect of stirring the country to a degree of excitement, whose direction and end it is not easy to foresee. Mr. Lowe's speech shows that a section at least already refu3es to be satisfied with even Mr. Glad- stone's programme. The Government may well look to it, and heed the signs of the times. We would warn them that timely concession to the voice of the people, which, in this case, is the voice of God, is the only way to expiate the terrible and costly errors of the past. Mr. Lowe has said that "the conscience of England is uneasy," and that conscience must be satisfied at all hazards.

div.head: EASTERN AFFAIRS.
div.p: EASTERN AFFAIRS.

Tura important event of the week in relation to the terrible Eastern imbroglio is the granting by Turkey of an armistice. The bloody business which has horrified Europe is temporarily at an end ; thanks to toe foreign minister and still more thanks to the hurricane of what Lord Beaconsfield am- biguously designates as the •‘ sublime en- thusiasm" of the English nation. It may be fairly doubted if even Lord Derby would have been able to drag, even for an hour, the sanguinary hand of the Turk from the throat of his victim, had it not been for the omnipotent humanity of England. The latest report from Turkey states that :

o definite terms of peace have been laid before the Bervian Government on the part of Great Britain as representing the mediating Powers, and there is a general expectation that the suspension of hostilities will be prolonged, in order to give the diplomatists time to enter upon negotiations. The proclamation of Prince Milan as King of Servia by the army was not, on the whole, received with disfavour at Belgrade. A deputation of all branches of the service has been sent from Deligrad to the Prince to salute him as King ; and the Time correspondent at headquarters says that in the highest quarters the probability of the armistice ending in a permanent peace is openly ridiculed. The Austrian correspondent of the same journal maintains that Tchernayeff is absolute master of the situation.

The affected incredulity of the Govern- ment on the subject of the Bulgarian hor- rors has been rudely invaded by the report of Mr. Baring, who—although he extenu- ates as much as possible the atrocities of the iurkish Paellas, is nevertheless constrained substantially to confirm the frightful narra- tives of the .Daily News correspondent.
